intro: のに is の (which turns a clause into a thing) + に, and it has two separate jobs. After any clause it means "even though": the facts went against what you expected, and you usually feel something about it. After a dictionary-form verb, followed by 使う, 便利, 必要 or かかる, it means "for doing". Look at what comes after のに to tell them apart.

skills.rule: A のに B: A is true, yet B happens against expectation, usually with surprise, regret or complaint.
skills.explain:
のに connects like ので: plain verbs and i-adjectives directly (行ったのに, 高いのに), nouns and na-adjectives with な (日曜日なのに, 静かなのに). 学生だのに is wrong.

It carries feeling: disappointment, frustration, surprise. 約束したのに来なかった is not just "he promised but didn't come" but "he promised, and he didn't come!". At the end of a sentence のに means "if only" or "but I ...": 言ってくれればよかったのに "You should have told me."

The edge: B must be a fact that has happened or is happening. のに cannot be followed by a request, command, invitation or intention (雨なのに行きましょう is wrong). For those, use けど or ても: 雨でも行きましょう. For a hypothetical "even if", always use ても. For a neutral "but" with no feeling, use けど or が.

examples.jp: 日曜日[にちようび]な{のに}、父[ちち]は会社[かいしゃ]に行[い]きました。
examples.en: My father went to work even though it was Sunday.

examples.jp: 薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだ{のに}、まだ頭[あたま]が痛[いた]いです。
examples.en: I took medicine, but my head still hurts.

examples.jp: この店[みせ]は高[たか]い{のに}、あまりおいしくない。
examples.en: This place is expensive, yet the food isn't very good.

examples.jp: 約束[やくそく]した{のに}、田中[たなか]さんは来[き]ませんでした。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka didn't come, even though he promised.

examples.jp: 一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]練習[れんしゅう]した{のに}、負[ま]けてしまった。
examples.en: We lost even though we practised so hard.

examples.jp: 言[い]ってくれればよかった{のに}。

contrast.note: けど is a neutral "but" and can be followed by a request or a plan. のに adds frustration or surprise and needs a fact after it.
ても is "even if" and works for hypotheses and plans: 雨が降っても行く. のに is for things that really happened: 雨が降ったのに行った.
ので is the reverse logic: B follows naturally from A. 練習したので勝った "we practised, so we won"; 練習したのに負けた "we practised, yet we lost".

mistakes.bad: 雨[あめ]なのに、出[で]かけましょう。
mistakes.good: 雨[あめ]でも出[で]かけましょう。
mistakes.note: のに cannot introduce an invitation or a plan. For "even if it rains, let's go", use ても.

mistakes.bad: 学生[がくせい]だのに、よく働[はたら]きます。
mistakes.good: 学生[がくせい]な{のに}、よく働[はたら]きます。
mistakes.note: After a noun or na-adjective, のに takes な, not だ.

mistakes.bad: 一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]練習[れんしゅう]したので、負[ま]けました。
mistakes.good: 一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]練習[れんしゅう]した{のに}、負[ま]けました。
mistakes.note: Losing goes against what practice should bring. That is のに, not a reason ので.

skills.tip: Can you add "and yet!" with a sigh? のに. Is the second half a request, a plan or an "even if"? Then it's not のに.

skills.rule: Dictionary-form verb + のに + 使う / 便利だ / 必要だ / いい / かかる means "for doing".
skills.explain:
The verb is always in the dictionary form: 切るのに, 行くのに. The predicate after it is one of a small set that judges use, usefulness or cost: 使う, 役に立つ, 便利だ, いい, 必要だ, 向いている, and かかる for time or money: 駅まで行くのに二十分かかる "it takes twenty minutes to get to the station".

With a noun you drop the の and use plain に: 料理に使う, 旅行に必要だ. 料理のに is wrong.

The edge: for the goal of a deliberate action (saving, studying, going somewhere), use ために, not のに: 家を買うために貯金している. のに only works when the main predicate is one of the usefulness or cost words above. には is close and is often interchangeable before 便利 or 必要, but には also introduces advice or requirements (痩せるには運動するしかない), where のに is impossible.

To tell it from "although": purpose のに follows a dictionary-form verb and is followed by one of these predicates, with no contrast between the halves.
patterns: [dictionary-form verb] のに [time / money] が かかる
[dictionary-form verb] のに 便利だ / 必要だ / いい

examples.jp: このナイフは肉[にく]を切[き]る{のに}使[つか]います。
examples.en: This knife is used for cutting meat.

examples.jp: 駅[えき]まで行[い]く{のに}、二十分[にじゅっぷん]かかります。
examples.en: It takes twenty minutes to get to the station.

examples.jp: この辞書[じしょ]は漢字[かんじ]を調[しら]べる{のに}便利[べんり]です。
examples.en: This dictionary is handy for looking up kanji.

examples.jp: この公園[こうえん]は子[こ]どもを遊[あそ]ばせる{のに}いいです。
examples.en: This park is good for letting children play.

examples.jp: 家[いえ]を建[た]てる{のに}、たくさんのお金[かね]が必要[ひつよう]です。
examples.en: You need a lot of money to build a house.

contrast.note: ために marks the goal of a deliberate action: 家を買うために貯金する. のに only goes with usefulness or cost predicates: 使う, 役に立つ, 便利, 必要, いい, かかる.
Before 便利 or 必要 the two are usually interchangeable. には can also introduce advice or a requirement (行くには予約が要る / 痩せるには運動するしかない); のに cannot.
After a noun there is no の: 料理に使う, 旅行に必要だ. のに is for a verb: 料理をするのに使う.

mistakes.bad: 家[いえ]を買[か]うのに、毎月[まいつき]貯金[ちょきん]しています。
mistakes.good: 家[いえ]を買[か]う{ために}、毎月[まいつき]貯金[ちょきん]しています。
mistakes.note: Saving is a deliberate action aimed at a goal, so the goal takes ために. のに needs 使う, 便利, 必要 or かかる after it.

mistakes.bad: この鍋[なべ]はカレーのに使[つか]います。
mistakes.good: この鍋[なべ]はカレーを作[つく]る{のに}使[つか]います。
mistakes.note: のに follows a verb. After a noun use plain に (カレーに使う), or add a verb as here.

mistakes.bad: この紙[かみ]は手紙[てがみ]を書[か]いたのに使[つか]います。
mistakes.good: この紙[かみ]は手紙[てがみ]を書[か]く{のに}使[つか]います。
mistakes.note: Purpose のに takes the dictionary form, never the past.

skills.tip: Is the sentence about what something is used for, good for, or costs? Dictionary-form verb + のに. A goal you are working towards takes ために.
